damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Hagrid's backstory explanation at the Leaky Cauldron
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 13–19: Hagrid gives a rich, emotionally textured account of Voldemort's rise, describing the terror of the dark times, the courage of the resistance, the specific deaths of the McKinnons, Bones, and Prewetts, Voldemort's growing power, and his own grief at knowing Harry's parents personally. He also explains that Voldemort was getting 'more an' more powerful' and nobody knew why he vanished.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3 compresses this into a few lines: 'Voldemort started ter gather some followers, brought 'em over to the dark side. Anyone that stood up to 'im ended up dead. Your parents fought against him, but nobody lived once he decided ter kill 'em. Nobody, not one. 'Cept you.' The texture of the dark times, the named victims, the political fear, and Hagrid's personal grief are almost entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this scene to establish Voldemort as a historically real terror with named victims and a society-wide impact. The film reduces him to a one-line villain backstory, stripping the audience's understanding of the stakes and Voldemort's scale of evil.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Hagrid's explanation of what happened to Voldemort after Godric's Hollow
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 22: Hagrid says Voldemort 'Disappeared. Vanished. Same night he tried ter kill you,' framing this as 'the biggest myst'ry' and noting Voldemort was getting more and more powerful, making his disappearance all the more inexplicable and ominous.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 5: Hagrid says 'some say 'e died. Codswallop, in my opinion. Nope, I reckon 'e's out there still, too tired ter carry on.' This flattens the mystery into a mundane 'too tired' explanation, removing the sense of inexplicable, terrifying mystery around Voldemort's fate.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's framing of Voldemort's disappearance as an unsolved mystery deepens his threat. The film's 'too tired to carry on' diminishes him from an inexplicable dark force to something merely exhausted, reducing his mystique and menace early in the saga.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 – Mirror of Erised / Quirrell confrontation, Voldemort's manipulation tactics
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 85–89: Voldemort speaks from the back of Quirrell's head. He attempts to manipulate Harry with philosophical arguments ('There is no good and evil, there is only power'), claims Harry's father 'put up a courageous fight,' says his mother 'needn't have died,' and tries to use Harry's grief as a lever. He also lies that his parents 'died begging me for mercy,' provoking Harry to shout 'LIAR!' — a key moment of Harry's moral courage and defiance.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 7: Voldemort similarly uses the 'no good and evil, only power' line and offers to bring Harry's parents back by showing them in the mirror. However, the specific lie that they 'died begging for mercy' — and Harry's furious, grief-driven rebuttal — is absent. Instead Harry simply says 'You liar!' in response to the parents-in-mirror manipulation, which is a weaker, less specific confrontation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's exchange gives Harry a specific, morally charged moment of defiance based on knowledge of his parents' courage. The film's version is vaguer, reducing Harry's act of resistance from a principled refutation of a specific lie to a generic rejection, weakening the emotional and moral core of the climax.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 – Voldemort's face and mode of speech on back of Quirrell's head
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 83–95: Voldemort speaks at length from the back of Quirrell's head in full sentences, philosophizes, taunts, commands ('SEIZE HIM!', 'KILL HIM!', 'Then kill him, fool, and be done!'), and is a distinct, terrifying presence controlling Quirrell. His chalk-white face with red eyes and snake-like nostrils is described. The interplay between Voldemort's commands and Quirrell's physical actions is extended and dramatic.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 7: Voldemort's face is shown on the back of Quirrell's head, but he speaks far fewer lines. Most of his dialogue is condensed. He says 'Stop him!' and 'Kill him!' but the extended back-and-forth of Voldemort's taunting, philosophizing, and commanding is shortened. Quirrell's physical deterioration under Harry's touch is also shortened — he crumbles quickly rather than the prolonged struggle of the book.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Voldemort's extended taunting in the book establishes his voice — cold, philosophical, cruel, manipulative — for the first time. The compressed film version gives audiences far less exposure to his distinct personality, making his first 'real' appearance less impactful as a character introduction.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 – Dumbledore's hospital wing explanation to Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 98–104: Dumbledore tells Harry to 'always use the proper name for things. Fear of a name increases fear of the thing itself' — a thematic statement directly about Voldemort. He also explains that Voldemort 'shows just as little mercy to his followers as his enemies,' left Quirrell to die, and that he 'is still out there somewhere, perhaps looking for another body to share.' He explicitly states Voldemort 'cannot be killed' in his current state. He also deflects Harry's question about why Voldemort wanted to kill him, saying Harry will know 'when you are ready.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 7: Dumbledore's explanation is shorter. The 'fear of a name' speech is entirely absent. The detail that Voldemort abandoned Quirrell to die and shows no mercy to followers is omitted. Dumbledore says 'I'm afraid there are ways in which he can return' but does not elaborate on Voldemort's nature (not truly alive, cannot be killed). The question of why Voldemort targeted Harry is not raised in this scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The 'fear of a name' lesson is one of the most thematically resonant moments in the book, directly tied to Harry's defining trait of naming Voldemort aloud. Its absence means the film never articulates this theme, and Dumbledore's characterization as a wise, principled mentor who shapes Harry's courage is weakened. The loss of Voldemort's ruthlessness toward his own followers also flattens his menace.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 – Common room scene, Hermione reassures about Dumbledore
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 55: Hermione says 'everyone says Dumbledore's the only one You-Know-Who was ever afraid of. With Dumbledore around, You-Know-Who won't touch you.' This is a brief reassurance, but in the book it is contextualised within a longer, exhausted, frightened conversation among all three friends about the full implications of what Harry saw.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 6: Hermione delivers almost the same lines — 'Who's the one wizard Voldemort always feared? Dumbledore. As long as Dumbledore is around, Harry, you're safe. As long as Dumbledore is around, you can't be touched.' However, this lands as overconfident foreshadowing since the very next scene has Dumbledore absent, making Hermione look naïve. In the book her reassurance is one note in a more complex, fearful conversation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor damage: the film version makes Hermione's reassurance slightly more absolute and dramatically ironic in a way that undercuts her characterisation as careful and intelligent, though the effect is small and the scene largely faithful.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Ollivander's, 'He-Who-Must-Not-Be-Named did great things'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus does not include the Ollivander scene in detail, but Film Scene 2 has Ollivander say 'We do not speak his name' and refer to Voldemort only as 'He-Who-Must-Not-Be-Named,' reflecting the wizarding world's fearful avoidance of the name.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 2: Ollivander refuses to name Voldemort and says 'He-Who-Must-Not-Be-Named did great things. Terrible, yes, but great.' While this is largely consistent with wizarding world fear norms, Ollivander's refusal to name Voldemort is slightly at odds with the book's establishment (Scene 5) that Dumbledore insists on using the name — setting up a world-building norm of fear that the film then does not complicate with Dumbledore's counter-lesson, since that lesson is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: On its own this scene is faithful to the wizarding world's fear norm. Its damage is indirect: without Dumbledore's 'fear of a name' corrective later, the film only shows the fearful norm and never challenges it thematically, leaving Ollivander's refusal as the last word on the subject.

main_damage_causes: Removal of Dumbledore's 'fear of a name' teaching strips the thematic and philosophical framing of Harry's defining habit of naming Voldemort, leaving the motif present in the film but unexplained and unanchored.

Compression of Hagrid's backstory eliminates the historical scale of Voldemort's terror — named victims, societal fear, the mystery of his disappearance — reducing him from a historically real catastrophe to a generic villain origin, weakening the audience's understanding of the stakes.

Truncation of the Mirror of Erised confrontation reduces Voldemort's first direct appearance as a speaking character: his philosophical voice, his specific cruelty toward Harry's parents, and Harry's principled moral defiance are all diminished, making his debut less impactful and Harry's courage less clearly earned.
